blocks.label: Lecture overview and learning outcomes
blocks.content: Okay. Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the fifth lecture of the Cancer Biology series. Today, we're going to think a little bit more about cancer evolution. So we've provided you with a framework now of how to think about cancer, that you get these progressively invasive growths that have acquired mutations, that those mutations have been caused by all sorts of environmental and other factors, and that those cells have then acquired the hallmarks whereby they are able to invade and spread and cause all sorts of problems. And we're going to add some layers onto that now and think about how the microenvironment might help to shape some of those processes, think about the types of cells which are maybe more predisposed to developing into these cancers, and to think about the evolution of this process and how it maybe occurs and adapts to its environment rather than being a well-defined and well-ordered process. So by the end of today's lecture, I hope that you will be able to illustrate the mechanisms by which cancer might develop, that you will be able to appraise the theory of Darwinian evolution as it applies to cancer, and recognize the importance of the immune system and other cells in the tumor microenvironment or the incipient tumor microenvironment that may be contributing to cancer growth.
blocks.why: The lecturer welcomes the class and outlines the topics and learning outcomes for the lecture.

blocks.label: Clonal expansion and Darwinian selection in cancer development
blocks.content: So, of course, a lot of the studies that we've done to date have come from doing sequencing of tumors and pre-neoplastic states. And there are a variety of different cancers, of course, and many of them show these sort of pre-neoplastic stages, some of which we can get hold of from tissue sections and study the genetics of. And through doing this, we're able to show that we go from this sort of normal cell to slightly more abnormal, to even more abnormal, to eventually becoming invasive and malignant. And to try and understand what contributes to this change, we can look at all these sort of pre-malignant stages, whether they're prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia that you saw in your practical. But there are these pre-stages, and we can look at them and try and work out what mutations do we see here at these early stages, and what do we see at these later stages, and try and put together a history of what might have happened. And of course, we know from studying adenocarcinoma and the adenomas that there are perhaps a sequence of changes and a number of signaling pathways that need to be disruptive so that those cells can invade and grow out. And we know, for example, that if you look at adenomas, about 80% of adenomas will have a mutation in APC. So that suggests that this is quite an early event that's acquired much earlier on, affecting the beta-catenin pathway, and that later on, we see more adenocarcinomas that have mutations in pathways such as p53. So 43% of adenocarcinomas will have lost tp53, and that there's something that goes on in between, whereby we gradually acquire further mutations. But these may not happen in this distinct order. We sort of make assumptions that there is a gradual loss of or gain of activity of certain pathways, and we try and put that together based on what we see in these pre-malignant stages compared to the invasive growth. But ultimately, what this suggests, that there's a certain level of evolution which is going on. So you can imagine a scenario where you start off with a cell that picks up a mutation, and that mutation is denoted here by this red quadrant, and that this cell maybe clonally expands because maybe that first mutation was in a protein that gave it a growth advantage over its neighbors. And so it fills more of the space in the tissue. And then you can imagine a situation whereby they may pick up, one of those cells may pick up a second mutation and a third mutation, a fourth mutation, and so on. So that we have this clonal succession whereby cells generally become fitter with each mutation that they pick up, and these fitter clones then contribute to making up more of the tissue space. We assume that maybe this happens every 10 to the sixth cell divisions but we don't really know that. Although now, of course, technologies are getting much better, so with single cell sequencing, we're able to infer times to when these mutations might be acquired. But you could also imagine a scenario where if these mutations that happen early on are in DNA repair genes, for example, that these successive clonal steps might occur much quicker. But ultimately, we have this process of natural selection, where clones which are fitter are the ones that predominate. And there have been studies which have shown this. So this was a study looking at the mouse esophagus. And what they did is they either randomly labeled cells with GFP, so they could monitor these cells in the mouse esophagus over time. And when they did this, you could see that the cells which were labeled with GFP, they didn't really expand or grow out. You might have got these little subclonal growths here, but eventually, you had this sort of up and down of different clones of cells, but nothing was particularly being selected for. Now, if they tagged that GFP onto the back of an oncogene, then they could show very clearly that the cells which were expressed in the oncogene, which they could see through the GFP expression, started to expand to the point where at one year they were filling up most of the esophagus. So this suggests that this oncogene is giving those cells a clonal advantage, a selective advantage, whereby they grow into the tissue space. They're able to essentially, misplace or- Grow into the tissue space where the other cells would have been that are less fit, if you like, to eventually predominate. So this was really quite nice experimental evidence that a oncogene, switching on oncogene could give clonal dominance to a particular cell type. This same group then went on to do another study, and what they did was they took eyelid skin from old people, healthy eyelid skin, other than it being, of course, from an aged person, and they sequenced little regions of the tissue. And what they did was map where they saw mutations in that tissue. So they were looking in particular at driver mutational events. So they looked for things like loss of P53 or gain of function in fibroblast growth factor receptor. And they mapped within these one centimeter squared tissue spaces of where they saw those mutations. And what they found is those that had sort of driving oncogenic events, such as FGFR3 here, filled up larger areas of the tissue space. So very much similar to what we saw with the esophagus in the mouse. The cells which have the mutation are perhaps dominant in growth and can take up more of the tissue space. But they also could see that in some spaces there were cells that had more than one mutation. So there were cells, for example, if we look at this one here, that has a mutation in FAT, that then also picked up a mutation in NOTCH1, also RBM10. So this successive clonal expansion where we have larger areas with more mutations. But they're still not developing into cancers. So this suggests that you can have tissue spaces where there may be is a clonal advantage, but that's not quite enough. There's not quite enough for those to grow out into cancers. Of course, you could imagine a scenario as well whereby if they are taking up more space and they're more predominant with any particular tissue, there's a more greater likelihood that they are going on to pick up more mutations, particularly, for example, UV exposure, if we think about skin cancer and this being the eyelid. So over time, they may pick up more UV-induced mutations which enable that expansion. But it suggests there's something else that's needed as well. You can't just have a cell with lots of mutations. So there's clearly a competitive fitness relative to other mutant clones because they start to take up more space, but they haven't quite got to that stage where they can become invasive growth. So what else do we need to happen? But what we could show from all of these experiments was that tumors develop by successive clones with more mutations which make them fitter. And these additional mutations give them a selective advantage over their neighbors. So this suggests we have sort of Darwinian evolution occurring on a micro scale, where we're selecting for the fittest clones, the clones, the sub clones which will enable progression of a cancer. And of course, this evidence comes from the fact that when we look in those different populations of cells, we see that they all share the same mutation, which suggests, of course, that they are clonal.
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how successive genetic mutations confer a competitive growth advantage to clones in tissue spaces.

blocks.label: Epigenetic plasticity in tumor initiation
blocks.content: But what about epigenetics? Epigenetics must also play a role, right? And you've seen that in your earlier lectures, that we can switch genes on and off with epigenetics. So is it not just the case that we have changes in genes where we are seeing mutations which enable cells to have different properties? But what if we're also changing the epigenetic landscape in these cells and we're changing the number of genes which are available to be transcribed, but in the absence of any mutational processes? And there was a study that came out a couple of years ago now where they did just this. What they thought is that, well, what if we just transiently switch off some of these epigenetic mechanisms? And so they used the fruit fly Drosophila as their model, and they transiently switched off the polycomb repressive complex. And when they transiently switch this off, and what polycomb repressive complex does is it maintains these regions of heterochromatin so that there is no transcription of the genes in that region. And what they found is loss of this, transient loss of this opened up the chromatin, enabled transcription of genes, which would then allow the cells to go on and pick up the hallmarks of cancer and transform into cancers. Importantly, they couldn't restore PRC expression and reverse tumor fate, which suggests even this transient change in the transcriptional landscape, the genes that were available to be transcribed could contribute to tumor development. So this opens up the whole idea that it's not just about mutations in genes, but also the transcriptional status of cells. And of course, the transcriptional status of cells can be strongly affected by the environment in which they're in.
blocks.why: The lecturer presents experimental evidence from Drosophila showing that transient epigenetic dysregulation alone can induce tumorigenesis.

blocks.label: Cell of origin and the cancer stem cell model
blocks.content: So is the cell of origin also important? Is it important what cell type these mutations are occurring in and maybe what their transcriptional landscape looks like at any point in time? And of course, normal healthy tissues develop through a very strict hierarchy. We have stem cells, tissue-specific stem cells. We have committed progenitors, and then we have our differentiated functional cell types. And you can imagine a situation where in a cancer, you might have also a similar hierarchy. So is there any evidence that this might be occurring in cancer? Because of course, the other thing is that cancers-- sorry, tissue-specific stem cells have this stemness capacity, and that's lost as cells differentiate. So if these cells already have the ability to self-renew, you might think they're already one step further to developing all the hallmarks of cancer. And actually, if we look at the hallmarks of stem cells, tissue-specific stem cells, we see a lot of similarities between tissue-specific stem cells and cancer cells. So these are the so-called hallmarks of stem cells, and there are a number of features here which you can see overlap with cancer. So one here being transplantability. You should be able to move a stem cell into another immunocompatible mouse, and it should be able to give rise to the full progeny of that stem cell. Similarly, one of the defining features of cancer in a mouse model is that you can transplant it into another mouse and it will give rise to a cancer. Of course, that would be an immunocompatible mouse. Is there niche dependency? We know that stem cells sit in a certain niche environment, and that niche environment, in a way, could control stem cell divisions and stem cell differentiation. So is there a similar effect going on in cancer? And we'll come onto that. Self-renewal, of course, the key feature of stem cells, tissue-specific stem cells. Presumably, this is also a feature that we need in our cancer cells because they need to be able to propagate and keep growing these masses. Multipotency, so the ability to give rise to differentiated progeny. Is this also a capacity that cancer cells have? Because when we look at cancer cells under the microscope, they don't necessarily all look the same, and they may be in different states of transition at any one time. Some maybe look more differentiated, some less differentiated, and you saw those colorectal adenocarcinomas where we had moderately differentiated, well differentiated. So that also suggests there's not only a level of multipotency, but also plasticity in those cancers, much like we expect of our tissue-specific stem cells. Of course, there are some differences, and it's pretty clear that cancer cells don't maintain genomic integrity like tissue-specific stem cells have to because these are our long-lived cells, and we need to protect them. So is a stem cell a prime target for developing into a cancer because it's already on its way to picking up some of those cancer hallmarks? And of course, if we think about normal stem cell division, it's really tightly controlled, and we can get asymmetric cell division whereby our stem cell can develop another stem cell and give rise to a daughter cell, if you like. So there are these very controlled processes where we have growth being just right. Not too many post-mitotic differentiated cells. We keep enough stem cells to fuel the growth of our tissue, but it's all very tightly regulated. So is this also the case in cancer? And of course, we know that stem cell hierarchy isn't that simple in most tissues. We know that there are also other levels of differentiation that occur in tissues. So in many tissues, we also have these transit amplifying progenitor cells. And of course, these are the cells which are sort of moving from having this self-renewal capacity to being differentiated post-mitotic cells, which are destined to die at some point. And there are increasing levels of their capacity to self-renew and, sorry, decreasing levels and increasing levels of their ability to differentiate. So where in this sort of normal hierarchy does a cancer initiate? Does it initiate in these cells up here which have already got some of those properties, or is it the case that we also see some dedifferentiation occurring and there is some evidence that even in normal tissue structure and tissue hierarchy, there is the capacity for plasticity where some cells may be able to dedifferentiate. So does this also happen in cancer? Do we have cells reacquiring stemness properties? And so this gives rise to the sort of two models of cancer development, which aren't mutually exclusive. So we have the stochastic model where we just have lots of clones of cells, some are fitter than others. But ultimately, you could take any one of those populations of cells and you could regrow a tumor, and some of those tumors might be more aggressive than others because they've picked up different properties. In the cancer stem cell model, you have a subpopulation of cells, much like in normal tissue hierarchy, and it's this subpopulation of cancer stem cells which is really driving tumor growth. They're the ones that not only give rise to other cancer stem cells but also give rise to what you might call the differentiated progeny of the tumor. But of course, it's not mutually exclusive, as I said, because you may also have cancer stem cells developing in this sort of stochastic manner. So what's the evidence for there being cancer stem cells? And the most of the evidence comes from our studies of leukemia, because leukemia, we can very easily compare that back to the normal hierarchy of hematopoiesis. So of course, as part of hematopoiesis, you have stem cells in the blood, and those stem cells will migrate out of the bone marrow and into tissue spaces, where in response to their microenvironment and other factors, they will then differentiate into the specialized cell types. So is it the case that leukemia develops from this cancer, this blood stem cell here, this hematopoietic stem cell? So there were some studies done quite a long time ago now where they took leukemia and they looked to see if they could find any cells within the whole population of leukemia that looked anything like a tissue-specific CD34 positive hematopoietic stem cell. And what they did was isolate those different cell populations. So they took the cells which looked like hematopoietic stem cells in that they expressed CD34, which is a marker of an hematopoietic stem cell, but they didn't express CD38, which is a protein which gets switched on as the cells differentiate. And when they took the 34 positive cells and put them into mice, they got tumors, and these are immunodeficient mice. These are human leukemias. They grew. But when they put the cells from the bulk population, so the 34 negative cells, they didn't get tumors. So this suggests that the cancer stem cell does exist in leukemias, that it's a discrete population of cells that has stemness capacity, the ability to differentiate, and produces the bulk leukemia. And there are cells there as well which are more differentiated that have lost that capacity. So this suggests there is some sort of hierarchy going on there in at least some leukemias. And of course, there are multiple different types of leukemias. But of course, those leukemias don't look like stem cells. They look more like the differentiated progeny, so they do retain the ability to differentiate. So there is still that plasticity there. So you will hear lots of names given to these cells within a cancer, and I think sometimes people are talking about the same thing and sometimes I think we're all talking about different things. And you may hear some people call them cancer stem cells, and that's because they are tissue-specific stem cells that have become transformed. You will hear some people call them tumor-propagating cells because otherwise cancer stem cells make it sound like it's a tissue-specific stem cell that's become transformed. But actually, in some cases, it's been shown that you can have a more differentiated cell type that's reacquired stemness. So we like to call them tumor-propagating cells. And you may also hear some people say tumor-initiating cells, although to me, the tumor-initiating cell is the cell right at the very beginning rather than the one that's propagating the established growth. So we have to think therefore that there is perhaps a hierarchy, at least in some cancers, and the evidence is maybe strongest in leukemia.
blocks.why: The lecturer explores stem cell hierarchies and evaluates evidence for cancer stem cells, focusing on leukemia.

blocks.label: Bottom-up transformation in colorectal adenomas
blocks.content: What about other cancers? What about cancers where the hierarchy, the normal tissue hierarchy, is perhaps less convoluted? So let's go back to the adenoma adenocarcinoma model and think about that. So if we look at the normal crypts of the intestine, you know that the stem cells all sit at the base here, and you can identify those cells because they express a protein called LGR5, which is a receptor for Wnt. And they sit in the base there alongside paneth cells, and paneth cells are basically supportive cells that support them in this stem cell state by providing Wnt. And as these cells differentiate, they move up the crypt where they are transit amplifying cells, and in this process, they lose stemness and become differentiated cells. And of course, this is a very well-controlled process, so we have just the right number of cells in our crypt. Now, there was a group that did a really quite elegant study where they took a mouse and they genetically engineered this mouse so they could switch off APC. And remember, APC mutation is one of the most common events in adenoma, suggesting it's an early initiation event. So they switched off APC, but they switched it off in defined cell types. They either switched it off just in these LGR5 positive stem cells or they switched it off just in these transit amplifying cells. And then they left the mice to see if they developed cancer. And what they found is if they switched it off in these transit amplifying cells, they occasionally saw these microadenomas, which you'll now be able to recognize after your histopathology classes, but really the tissue looked relatively normal. But when they switched it off in the stem cells, the LGR5 positive cells, they then started to see these really rather large adenomas, suggesting that this mutation happening in stem cells is perhaps a more predisposing because you've got adenomas now more chance of them picking up mutations and becoming adenocarcinomas. So they termed this bottom-up transformation. So saying that the whole process of colorectal adenocarcinoma development actually must start, is more likely to start down here in these basal crypt stem cells. We're going to come back to this model. So how does this fit with the whole idea of evolution? Well, of course, as I said before, it's not mutually exclusive. And we know that this is a multistep process where cells gradually pick up mutations, and those mutations may well be picked up in these long-lived stem cell compartments. They hang around for a long time. They don't divide very often, but cancer is generally a disease of older age, so maybe that fits that we would have stem cells giving rise to cancer. But also, it's of course more complicated than that because we know that these stem cells give rise to transit amplifying cells and so on. And at each stage, these cells may then pick up mutations in later differentiated steps. And so it could also be the case that it may be as initiating event in stem cells, but actually the mutations that are then picked up aren't in the stem cells themselves, but in the more differentiated progeny that then give rise to cancer. So I guess what I'm trying to illustrate here is there's no one route to malignancy. There are potentially multiple pathways which could occur depending on the types of mutations that are picked up by these cells, the transcriptional landscape that's available in those cells, and what those cells are to begin with and the properties they may inherently have.
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses mouse models comparing the effect of APC deletion in intestinal stem cells versus transit amplifying cells.

blocks.label: Environmental promoters and macrophage signaling in lung cancer
blocks.content: So let's come back to that eyelid example. So why do these cells on the eyelid have all these mutations and these mutations give a sort of competitive advantage to those cells in that they grow up to fill more space, but why haven't they developed into cancer? So is it also the case that the microenvironment these cells are in have to be permissive as well as they have to be occurring in certain cell types? So maybe we're seeing these mutations in cell types which aren't going to go on and transform because they're terminally differentiated and haven't picked up stemness potential. But what if the microenvironment also has to be permissive? So is there a role as well, not just having these incipient cancer cells predisposed by having mutations, but that some environmental stimulus, most likely a microenvironmental stimulus, is also necessary to make the microenvironment conducive to enabling those cells to grow out and expand and invade. And I'm going to come back here to that asbestos example we had in the cancer causes lecture where we know that asbestos isn't a mutagen. And the idea that this is a promoter whereby perhaps we have cells which have mutations but they're not transforming and growing out into cancers because there's no promoter to drive their onward proliferation. And so perhaps the asbestos is providing that second microenvironmental hit that's enabling those cells to then grow out in their environment. So is there any other evidence towards this in actual cancers that we have this sort of initiator mutations in certain cell types and then promotional events which are conducive with malignant growth? And we're starting to see lung cancer in much younger people now, much like we're starting to see colon cancer in younger people now. And so there was this study published three years ago now where they wanted to try and understand why they were seeing cancer in younger people, lung cancer in particular. And they did this really nice study looking at healthy lung and also looking at lung cancers to try and work out what the conditions must be to drive cancer growth. And they showed that it was a combination of not just having cells that carry cancer-causing mutations, but the just right conditions have to be there. And their study proposed that the just right conditions were provided by a promoter in the form of inflammation caused by pollution. So basically what they came to was the idea that about 50% of normal lung carries mutations in K-RAS or EGFR, but those cells just sort of sit there. They don't do too much. They may fill up a little bit of space, but they don't invade and expand. You need a secondary promotional event that enables that, and it could be in the wider environment. And so they showed that pollution could provide this secondary activity, but in particular, it was the particulate matter in pollution that they saw. And that was because the particulate matter was being recruited by macrophages. So another cell type coming into the microenvironment of these mutated cells. So now we don't just have mutant cells, we also have macrophages that are there because they're trying to deal with the particulate matter that comes from pollution. And what are those macrophages doing? They're secreting IL-1B. And the cancer cells, the incipient cancer cells they showed had the receptor for IL-1B. And what they were able to show is that, that IL-1B was switching on a stem-like state in those incipient cancer cells. So this was a combination of things, not just having mutations in cells, but also having the right environment and in this case, not just the wider environment, but also the tumor microenvironment, and that these cells required some paracrine signaling to be able to grow out and to acquire this stem-like state and to develop into full malignancies. So both environmental and the induced microenvironment are necessary for lung cancer development in this particular situation. And you could also think that there might be scenarios where those environmental pollutions could also be mutagens. So a double whammy, not only just producing inflammation, but also having also further mutagenic activity. So we have this situation where we have mutant cells in the lung. These people are being exposed to this environmental pollution, that the particulate matter is driving this local inflammatory response, which is changing the way the cells behave by giving them this stem-like signature, which on top of this mutational pathway activating a growth factor is driving this malignancy.
blocks.why: The lecturer describes how particulate pollution triggers macrophage IL-1B secretion to induce a stem-like state in mutant lung cells.

blocks.label: Chronic inflammation and K-RAS activation in intestinal transformation
blocks.content: So if this is happening in lung cancer, is this happening in other cancers as well? And how does it then fit in with the whole stem cell idea and the clonal evolution? And I'm going to come back to this APC knockout mouse model where they knocked it out either in the basal crypt stem cells or in the transit amplifying cells. Now they thought, well, what if actually there has to be some sort of microenvironmental stimulus as well, because remember, they only developed adenomas. They didn't get adenocarcinomas, so clearly there's something else that's required. But what if there's something else which contributes to this? And of course, with colon cancer, we know that the colon, our intestines are exposed to all sorts of things. Not just their microbiome, but also there are all sorts of different things which go through in our diet. And we've talked about in our cancer causes lecture that there are some things, for example, in overcooked meat, there are some things, contaminants of peanuts. What if something else that goes through our intestines drives a chronic inflammatory response? So they thought, well, we'll model this, and we'll model this by essentially deleting APC in these transit amplifying cells or in these stem cells. But on top of this, we're going to feed the mice dextran sulfate. And what dextran sulfate does is it causes chronic inflammation in the colon, and it's been used for many years as a really good model to study colitis. So this is what they did. They fed the mouse dextran sulfate, and they waited to see what happened. And actually what they could find was that when they did this, these transit amplifying cells then went on to develop adenomas, much like we saw when you knocked out APC just in the stem cells. So now we have a scenario whereby if you knock it out APC in the stem cells, you get adenomas, but if you knock it out in the transit amplifying cells but then also provide a chronic inflammatory stimulus, now you do get adenomas developing where they didn't see that before in the absence of inflammation. They also back crossed it to a second mouse line, a mouse that has a mutation in the RAS pathway. And these also could develop cancers from this transit amplifying cell population when they had previously knocked out APC. So what is the mutant K-RAS doing that chronic inflammation is perhaps also doing? And what they proposed is this model here whereby normal inflammation produces things like TNF, and what TNF does is activate the NF-kappa B pathway. K-RAS can also do the same thing. It can bypass growth factor-driven signaling of NF-kappa B and come in directly and activate that pathway in the absence of any external stimulus. At the same time, by lacking APC, there's lots of free beta-catenin available in the cells. And that free beta-catenin binds with the NF-kappa B proteins to essentially drive transcription of a stem cell signature. So what's happened here is that we either have the scenario where we transform those cells in the base of the crypt. These are longer-lived cells. They already have a stem cell program. Or we can also develop cancer if we mimic that by essentially switching on a stem cell program through driving this chronic inflammatory process. So it's not just about having mutations, it's having mutations in the right cell type with the right properties at any one time. And some of those properties may be conferred by the mutations which are occurring, and some of them may be conferred by the external events, microenvironmental, environmental activities, whereby you end up with a situation where you have the just right conditions to enable malignant and invasive growth.
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how chronic inflammation and mutant K-RAS cooperate with APC loss via NF-kappa B and beta-catenin to drive transformation in transit amplifying cells.

blocks.label: Microenvironmental dependence of established tumors and therapeutic implications
blocks.content: So what about the established tumor? Because we know that in the established tumor, there are also all sorts of inflammatory cells and stromal cells. Is there a role for other cells in driving the growth of the established tumor, not just the incipient tumor? And there was a study that was done quite some time ago now, because we wouldn't be allowed to do this these days, where they took basal cell carcinomas, and you can see one here near this person's ear. And they took the basal carcinoma cells, and they transplanted them onto another site of the same person. And they only developed basal cell carcinomas at that second site if they also transplanted across the stromal cells and all the other cells in the tumor microenvironment. So if they just put the tumor cells there, it didn't expand into a tumor. So that suggests that actually, even though we like to think of cancers being quite autonomous for growth, they clearly still need that supportive structure. They clearly still need an inflammatory environment, perhaps a supportive stroma, which enables their growth. And it's likely there is some paracrine signaling there that facilitates that. But studies like this, of course, opened up all sorts of new areas when we think about therapy as well. Because there are lots of cells in the tumor microenvironment, and now this has given rise to an area of therapy where people are instead trying to block those supportive cells rather than kill the cancer cells directly. And of course, you heard in your immunology lectures about cancer immunotherapy, and we'll talk a little bit more about that on Monday. But also angiogenesis. Can we block angiogenesis? Can we block the growth stimulatory signals that come from things like cancer-associated fibroblasts? So there's a lot of work now looking at how we exploit the tumor microenvironment as well to prevent this sort of codependency between these populations.
blocks.why: The lecturer explains the requirement of stroma for established tumor growth and the therapeutic strategies targeting the tumor microenvironment.

blocks.label: Technologies for investigating tumor evolution and microenvironment
blocks.content: And so how are we doing this? How can we investigate this in the lab? Well, a lot of what I've shown you has come from mouse models, and these are mice or Drosophila. They're fruit flies. They're not human beings. But of course, we can't genetically manipulate people and see if they develop cancer. That's unethical. But we can get access to tissue specimens, and we can sequence those tissue specimens, and there are all sorts of bioinformatics, computational biology algorithms that can now be used to try and work out the timing of mutational events in tumor cells. So single-cell RNA and DNA sequencing are being increasingly used in that way, as is mathematical modeling. Of course, single-cell DNA sequencing is still pretty expensive, but single-cell RNA sequencing is coming down in cost. So we're now learning more and more about the plasticity of tumor cells and how they interact with their environment. And the other thing that's enabling to do that is the availability of things like spatial transcriptomics or proteomics. Because with spatial transcriptomics, we can take tissue sections of the cancer, and we can essentially look at the transcriptomes in different areas of that tissue section, and we can map those transcriptional programs to cells of which we already know what their transcriptional program is. So, for example, we can find areas of cells. Maybe there is lots of cells here which are producing lots of chemokines and have transcriptional programs that we generally see in lymphocytes. We can map within the tumor where all these different populations are. Similarly with proteomics, spatial proteomics, again, we can look and see where different populations of cells are sitting within the tumor and work out how they might be interacting with each other and what signals may be being passed between them that are conducive with malignant growth.
blocks.why: The lecturer describes analytical methods including single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics used to study tumor heterogeneity and cellular interactions.

blocks.label: Summary of multi-factor cancer evolution
blocks.content: So we're at the situation, I think, where there are potentially multiple routes to the same endpoint. And we like to think that we have this nice ordered process whereby we gradually pick up mutations and these affect key pathways and we get malignant outgrowth. But it's very clear that there's much more to it than that. There's also that microenvironmental influence. And chronic inflammation may be playing a role in many, if not a lot of different cancers in that these are the cells which are also producing lots of growth factors, chemokines, cytokines, for which tumor cells may have receptors, which may be enabling this process. We also have to think about the cell of origin and where all this is occurring. Is the cell in which these mutations are being picked up already halfway to becoming a cancer, in that they already have capacities like stem cells? They can already self-renew. They don't have to pick up that property. So that could also play a role in what types of cells we see and what tissues we see develop into cancer at different stages of life. And of course, this has implications as well when we think about childhood cancers, because childhood cancers occur very early in life when we're developing. When certain cell types are going through growth spurts, perhaps that puts them at a greater risk of picking up mutations and being in an environment which is conducive with malignancy. We also have to think about those wider environmental exposures and how they might be affecting the microenvironmental exposures. So as we talked about in the cancer causes lecture, there are lots of things we're exposed to that can cause mutations, but also lots of things that can cause chronic inflammation. So a combination of these things occurring in just the right scenarios is perhaps what's also driving this process. And as we saw in that lung cancer model, that exposure to those environmental pollutants is causing this chronic inflammatory response, changing the microenvironment those cells are sitting in, which makes them more prone, more predisposed to developing into malignancies. So when we think about cancer, we can't just think about mutations. We can't just think about the stepwise accumulation of mutations that confer the hallmark properties of cancer, which now enable invasion and malignant growth. We have to think about a combination of things and how much those factors coming together are creating an environment that's conducive with outgrowth of malignant clones. So there's probably a balance. It has to be just right. And if you just have these sort of pro-tumorigenic microenvironments, they maybe have to go on for a long time so that you pick up mutations if they are also acting as mutagens in some way. But you also have this mutational burden where you have cells which are picking up properties that make them predisposed to growth in the right microenvironment. And on top of all of that, there's also this idea, of course, that we're now having to see these changes in transcriptional state of the cells. And of course, cancers are highly plastic, as I said before. Are the cancer cells sort of flipping between plastic states dependent on their epigenetic, their epigenome, and how that might change and what's available to be transcribed at any point in time? So all of these things together have to occur at just the right time in just the right place. And so ultimately, you might consider that it's all down to evolution. The right situation arises where we have these fit clones of cells in the right environment that enables them to prosper. So, where are we? So hopefully you've seen we've added on another layer to what we've taught you so far. Cancer develops not just by picking up mutations and becoming fitter, but it's an evolutionary process with the acquisition of mutations that affect key pathways that allow cells to acquire the hallmarks of cancer. We know that mutations alone are probably insufficient for some cancers to develop. We also have to think also about the inherent properties of the cells in which those mutations are taking place. Do those cells already have some key cancer-promoting properties, such as the ability to self-renew? Are environmental promoters also playing a role in all of this? So not just environmental mutagens, but also factors which can promote cancer through developing chronic inflammation. And ultimately, there's likely to be some level of coevolution between these processes, where that tumor microenvironment or the environment of that incipient cancer cell that has mutations has to be just right to permit outgrowth and invasion.
blocks.why: The lecturer synthesizes how mutations, cell of origin, epigenetic plasticity, and the microenvironment converge in cancer development.

blocks.content: And with that, I will end today's lecture, and Monday we will talk about therapy.
